Here we show that the approach of combining physicsinformed machine learning,mechanistic modeling,and experimental data can reduce defects in AM by considering an example of a common balling defect in L-PBF. The physics of balling captured through the computed values of the mechanistic variables is analyzed by a physics-informed machine learning to correlate with the balling occurrence data of one hundred and sixty-six independent experiments for six commonly used alloys: AlSi10Mg [11], aluminum 357 [11],stainless steel 316 [12,13], Co-Cr [14], Ti6Al4V [15]and Inconel 718 [16].Based on this approach (Fig.1）of combining experimental data,mechanistic modeling,and physicsinformed machine learning,we develop an easy-to-use,verifiable balling susceptibility index that can be used to predict and prevent balling in L-PBF.In addition,we investigate the hierarchical importance of the mechanistic variables on balling and present balling susceptibility maps for six alloys.The approach used here can help to reduce other common defects in AM such as cracking，porosity,lack of fusion,and surface roughness for producing defect-free L-PBF components.

# Experimental Research on Selective Laser Melting AlSi10Mg Alloys: Process, Densification and Performance

Zhen Chen, Zhengying Wei, Pei Wei, Shenggui Chen, Bingheng Lu, Jun Du, Junfeng Li, and Shuzhe Zhang

(Submitted January 10, 2017; in revised form August 23, 2017; published online November 9, 2017)

In this work, a set of experiments was designed to investigate the effect of process parameters on the relative
density of the AlSi10Mg parts manufactured by SLM. The influence of laser scan speed v, laser power P and
hatch space H, which were considered as the dominant parameters, on the powder melting and densification
behavior was also studied experimentally. In addition, the laser energy density was introduced to evaluate
the combined effect of the above dominant parameters, so as to control the SLM process integrally. As a
result, a high relative density (> 97%) was obtained by SLM at an optimized laser energy density of 3.55.5 J/mm[2]. Moreover, a parameter–densification map was established to visually select the optimum process
parameters for the SLM-processed AlSi10Mg parts with elevated density and required mechanical properties. The results provide an important experimental guidance for obtaining AlSi10Mg components with
full density and gradient functional porosity by SLM.

Keywords selective laser melting, AlSi10Mg, densification,
energy density, processing parameters

IV. CONCLUSION

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

The presented results are based on work that was done for the
Bionic Aircraft project. This project has received funding from the
European Union’s Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Program
under Grant Agreement No. 690689.

In this study, the effect of the laser beam profile (the Gaussian
and Donut beam profiles) on the SLM process has been studied for
the aluminum alloy AlSi10Mg. The goal was to investigate if alternative beam profiles such as the Donut beam profile offer benefits
to the SLM process in terms of stability and productivity of the
process. Therefore, single tracks and density cubes were manufactured for different process parameters. For the single tracks, the
shape and size of the single tracks were analyzed based on their top
view and microsections. For the density cubes, the porosity and
types of defects were analyzed on microsections with respect to different key figures (LEDs, VEDs, and build rate). The most important findings can be summarized as follows:

- The process window that produces stable single tracks and cubes
with densities of >99.5% is larger for the Donut beam profile
than that for the Gaussian beam profile.

- The single tracks of the Donut beam profile are wider than that
of the Gaussian beam profile and the effect of the process parameters on the melt pool depth of the Donut beam profile is not as
significant as that of the Gaussian beam profile.

content:
High-quality manufacturing has particular importance in the Industry 4.0 era. Additive manufacturing (AM) is
among the core technologies of industry 4.0, and selective laser melting (SLM) is among its best techniques in
manufacturing of near-full dense parts. To ensure densification and porosity free products, the influence of
processing parameters and heat treatment conditions should be understood. The aim of this paper is to study the
effect of processing parameters and heat treatments such as T4 (solution heat treatment) and T6 (artificial aging)
on the densification and porosity of AlSi10Mg parts built by SLM. The results showed that the best densification
with minimum porosities was attained at the energy density of 144.89 J/mm[3]. It was confirmed from optical
microscopic and SEM images that highly dense parts had lower porosity. We have also optimized the processing
parameters by applying statistical analysis for the fabrication of fully dense components. Finally, it is concluded
that the densification is enhanced to 99.94% by applying T4-HT at 530 °C and 99.87% in T6-HT, and porosities
are also reduced by the heat treatments due to fine grain structure and strong bonding among the powder
particles.

There is an
interrelation between energy density and porosity, which means that
porosity can be reduced by utilizing a specific energy density range
(Peng & Chen, 2018). Porosities and density are also a sign of stability
and strength of any manufactured product for the manufacturing process. The porosities are generally categorized by the macro and micro
level porosities, and macro porosities create cracks in the SLM fabricated components, and micro porosities become more critical and
prominent after heat treatment processes (Galy, Le Guen, Lacoste, &
Arvieu, 2018). The densification and porosity are inter-connected to
each other; if the densification increases then the porosity reduces. The
densification of parts is decreased due to the insufficient melting and
poor interlayer metallurgical bonding of the powder particles during
the SLM fabrication. The variations in the densification are due to the
development of porosities, oxides particles, etc. in the parts. Higher
densification can be attained by the sufficient melting, good interlayer
metallurgical bonding of powder particles, and appropriately filling the
pores of the solid phase (Wang, Wang et al., 2017). So, fully-dense
density parts have better mechanical properties. Recently, Majeed,
Zhang, Lv, Peng, Waqar, and Atta (2018) investigated the influence of
processing parameters and heat treatments on the relative density of
AlSi10Mg alloy parts.

of high-energy laser scanning, there is a significant temperature
difference that forms from the center to the edge of the molten
pool’s surface. This temperature gradient leads to variations in
surface tension, causing the emergence of Marangoni convection. As a result of Marangoni flow, the molten material is
directed toward the central region of the pool, rather than
spreading outward across the underlying surface leading to
balling effect which is a typical metallurgical defect in powder
bed fusion process (Ref 17). Higher scan speeds can impose
increased shear stress on the liquid phase which generates
heightened surface tension within the melt pool, also increasing
the possibility of ball formation. The occurrence of liquid ball
splashes at higher scan speeds can further contribute to porosity
in such processing conditions (Ref 20, 21). Notably, both sample sets A and B experience a drop in
density at an LED of 0.45 J/mm and 0.381 J/mm, respectively. This is due to the increased scan rate that contributes to the
density reduction in laser-melted AlSi10Mg since it results in
insufficient energy input for complete powder melting and
partial re-melting of the substrate material, introducing irregularities (Ref 5). Figures 3 and 4 provide SEM micrographs illustrating the
cross sections of laser-melted samples, offering insight into the
distribution of porosity in both sample sets A and B.

The impact of nano-TiC particles on the microstructure of
SLM-fabricated specimens was investigated, with a focus on
sample A1. This specimen, produced using a laser power of
250 W, scanning speed of 680 mm/s, and a layer thickness of
30 lm, exhibited the highest relative density, lowest porosity,
and maximum hardness. In the works done by Gu et al. (Ref
17) it is seen that there are no major differences in the

microstructure of TiC-reinforced AlSi10Mg specimens with
varying LED as the dispersion of TiC was observed to be
uniform, but there was a noticeable variation in the size of the
TiC reinforcements at higher LED levels, primarily due to their
tendency to aggregate into clusters. This is attributed to the
emergence of Marangoni effect in the molten pool leading to
the generation of liquid capillary forces. This force, in turn,
exerts an influence on the TiC reinforcing particles, facilitating
their rearrangement within the pool.

The most economic way to get information about the quality of a SLMed part is the measurement

of powder metallurgy products. The relative density of parts has a close relationship with the existence
